title: The Man Who Survived Both Atomic Bombs
sources: Wikipedia, 'Tsutomu Yamaguchi' (Mitsubishi engineer, Hiroshima 6 Aug 1945 then Nagasaki 9 Aug; Japan recognised him as a double survivor in March 2009; died 4 Jan 2010 aged 93)
Biography.com, 'Tsutomu Yamaguchi: Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombing survivor' (about 3 km from each blast, boss disbelieved him, later nuclear-disarmament advocate)
RNZ, 'Tsutomu Yamaguchi: the man who survived both atomic bombs' (same account; dialogue is dramatized, not verbatim)

lines.text: a bandaged man walks into his office, and says a whole city is gone.
Nagasaki, August 1945. Engineer Tsutomu Yamaguchi has just crawled home from Hiroshima.
Days earlier, he was there on business, one train ride from home.
Then the sky flashed white, and the street he stood on was gone.
Burned and half deaf, he sheltered overnight, then took the first train out.
His boss stares at the bandages. "One bomb? One bomb destroyed a whole city?"
"Be reasonable. A single bomb cannot do that."
"I saw it. I was standing in it."
Then the office window turned white again.
Same man, three kilometres from the blast, a second time.
Picture lightning striking your roof twice in three days.
He lived to ninety-three, speaking out against nuclear weapons.
In 2009, Japan recognised him as a survivor of both bombs.
Unluckiest man alive? Or luckiest? People still argue.
So when you call yourself unlucky, remember that
